abstract: <jats:p>Activity of tonoplast slow vacuolar (SV, or TPC1) channels has to be under a tight control, to avoid undesirable leak of cations stored in the vacuole. This is particularly important for salt‐grown plants, to ensure efficient vacuolar Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> sequestration. In this study we show that choline, a cationic precursor of glycine betaine, efficiently blocks SV channels in leaf and root vacuoles of the two chenopods, <jats:italic>Chenopodium quinoa</jats:italic> (halophyte) and <jats:italic>Beta vulgaris</jats:italic> (glycophyte). At the same time, betaine and proline, two major cytosolic organic osmolytes, have no significant effect on SV channel activity. Physiological implications of these findings are discussed.</jats:p>
title: Choline but not its derivative betaine blocks slow vacuolar channels in the halophyte Chenopodium quinoa: Implications for salinity stress responses

abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p> <jats:bold>The C<jats:sub>3</jats:sub> halophyte <jats:italic>Suaeda salsa</jats:italic> was used to investigate the roles of Ca<jats:sup>2+</jats:sup>, Ca<jats:sup>2+</jats:sup> channels, and calmodulin (CaM) in betacyanin metabolism. Seeds of <jats:italic>S. salsa</jats:italic> were cultured in both the dark and light for 3 days. The fresh weight and betacyanin content were much higher in <jats:italic>S. salsa</jats:italic> seedlings formed in the dark than in seedlings formed in the light. The addition of Ca<jats:sup>2+</jats:sup> to the half‐strength MS nutrient solution promoted betacyanin accumulation in the dark, whereas Ca<jats:sup>2+</jats:sup> depletion by EGTA suppressed the dark‐induced betacyanin accumulation in shoots of <jats:italic>S. salsa</jats:italic>. The Ca<jats:sup>2+</jats:sup> channel blocker LaCl<jats:sub>3</jats:sub> also inhibited dark‐induced betacyanin accumulation. The highest activity of CaM and the maximum betacyanin content decreased by 51% and 45%, respectively, in shoots of <jats:italic>S. salsa</jats:italic> seedlings treated with the potent CaM antagonist chlorpromazine in the dark. Furthermore, the other CaM antagonist <jats:italic>N</jats:italic>‐(6‐aminohexyl)‐5‐chloro‐1‐naphthalenesulfonamide (W‐7) also inhibited the activity of CaM and dark‐dependent betacyanin accumulation, whereas its less active structural analog <jats:italic>N</jats:italic>‐(6‐aminohexyl)‐1‐naphthalenesulfonamide (W‐5) had little effect on the responses to dark of <jats:italic>S. salsa</jats:italic> seedlings. These results suggest that Ca<jats:sup>2+</jats:sup>, Ca<jats:sup>2+</jats:sup>‐regulated ion channels, and CaM play an important role in dark‐induced betacyanin accumulation in the shoots of the C<jats:sub>3</jats:sub> halophyte <jats:italic>S. salsa</jats:italic>.</jats:bold> </jats:p>

abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Plants are subjected to salt and drought stresses concurrently but our knowledge about the effects of combined stress on plants is limited, especially on halophytes. We aim to study if some diverse drought and salt tolerance traits in halophyte may explain their tolerance to salinity and drought stresses, individual and in combination, and identify key traits that influence growth under such stress conditions. Here, the halophyte <jats:italic>Halogeton glomeratus</jats:italic> was grown under control, single or combinations of 60 days drought and salt treatments, and morphophysiological responses were tested. Our results showed that drought, salinity, and combination of these two stressors decreased plant growth (shoot height, root length, and biomass), leaf photosynthetic pigments content (chlorophyll <jats:italic>a</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>b</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>a</jats:italic> + <jats:italic>b</jats:italic> and carotenoids), gas exchange parameters (Net photosynthesis rate [<jats:italic>P</jats:italic><jats:sub>N</jats:sub>], transpiration rate [<jats:italic>E</jats:italic>], stomatal conductance [<jats:italic>g</jats:italic><jats:sub>s</jats:sub>]), and water potential (<jats:italic>ψ</jats:italic><jats:sub>w</jats:sub>), and the decreases were more prominent under combined drought and salinity treatment compared with these two stressors individually performed. Similarly, combined drought and salinity treatment induced more severe oxidative stress as indicated by more hydrogen peroxide (H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>O<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>) and malondialdehyde (MDA) accumulated. Nevertheless, <jats:italic>H. glomeratus</jats:italic> is equipped with specific mechanisms to protect itself against drought and salt stresses, including upregulation of superoxide dismutases (SOD; EC 1.15.1.1) and catalase (CAT; EC 1.11.1.6) activities and accumulation of osmoprotectants (Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup>, Cl<jats:sup>−</jats:sup>, and soluble sugar). Our results indicated that photosynthetic pigments content, gas exchange parameters, water potential, APX activity, CAT activity, soluble sugar, H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>O<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>, and MDA are valuable screening criteria for drought and salt, alone or combined, and provide the tolerant assessment of <jats:italic>H. glomeratus</jats:italic>.</jats:p>
title: Negative effects of long‐term exposure to salinity, drought, and combined stresses on halophyte Halogeton glomeratus
